e-13192.problem: Sketch a representation of the set $S = \{1, 2\} \times (0, 1)$ in the Cartesian plane.
e-13192.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B = \big\{(a,b) \::\: a\in A,\, b\in B\big\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S = \{1,2\} \times (0,1)
$$

contains every point in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is either $1$ or $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(0,1).$

$$
S=
\Big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x\in \{{\color{red}{1}},{\color{blue}{2}}\},\, y\in (0,1) \Big\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider $S_1\subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals ${\color{red}{1}}$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(0,1).$

$$
S_1 = \Big\{ ({\color{red}{1}},y) \: : \: y \in(0,1) \Big\}
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040430/assets/56f200fce557749a56b9b5b51bc670da5f8c7f2cdb0196392ee80efcd6be980a.png)

Next, consider $S_2\subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals ${\color{blue}{2}}$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(0,1).$

$$
S_2 = \big\{ ({\color{blue}{2}},y) \: : \: y \in(0,1) \big\}.
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040430/assets/f96074cc265bba6eb59717364d2aa5390fdccea4d398fe5ae0b99f7ad82f0b93.png)

Our Cartesian product is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
S = S_1\cup S_2
$$

Therefore, $S$ can be represented by the two line segments shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040430/assets/0c0529aaa680b4b572d17f2cfbfb76d805134e72c50ab3ed469286cc025185a3.png)

e-13162.problem: Sketch a representation of the set $S = \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ in the Cartesian plane.
e-13162.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B = \big\{(a,b) \::\: a\in A,\, b\in B\big\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S = \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}
$$

contains every point in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is an integer number and whose $y$-coordinate is a natural number.

$$
S=
\Big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x\in \mathbb Z,\, y\in \mathbb N\Big\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider $S_1\subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any integer number and whose $y$-coordinate equals ${\color{red}{1}}.$

$$
S_1 = \Big\{ (x, {\color{red}{1}}) \: : \: x\in \mathbb Z\Big\}.
$$

We can represent $S_1$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040430/assets/6b63e973bbcc3e25d601a1f6cef97f5a00cc22e738c46d04a1ac06851421894e.png)

Next, consider $S_2\subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any integer number and whose $y$-coordinate equals ${\color{blue}{2}}.$

$$
S_2 = \Big\{ (x,{\color{blue}{2}}) \: : \: x\in \mathbb Z\Big\}.
$$

We can represent $S_2$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040430/assets/f24ce8f7610d096c795a8a74b0b714b720c36442042c28b66432d6b2102fb9d4.png)

We can create the subsets $S_3,S_4,S_5,\ldots,$ similarly. Our Cartesian product $S$ is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup {S}_{4}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in N}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ as the set of points in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040430/assets/c999c61d8ffbb27d47272811e32340cef3253b4730e684be10615487a8b27200.png)

e-13320.knowledge_point: Visualizing Unions of Uncountable Families of Indexed Sets
e-13320.problem: Sketch a representation of the set $\,\displaystyle \bigcup_{i \in I} X_i$ in the Cartesian plane given that $I = [-1,1] \subset \mathbb{R}$ and $X_i = \{ i \} \times [0, \, i^2].$
e-13320.worked_solution:
Recall that the union of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *at least one* set:

$$
\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \big\{ x \: : \: x \in A_k \:\:\textrm{for at least one}\:\: k \in I \big\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=-0.5,$ we have 

$$
X_{-0.5} = \{ -0.5 \} \times [0, 0.25] = \big\{ (-0.5,k) \: : \: k \in [0, 0.25] \big\}.
$$

This represents a vertical line segment from the point $(-0.5, 0)$ to the point $(-0.5,0.25)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040430/assets/ccc75eac899efcab1d0b6fde12609a3ea8f61d6fec74c739ef3393fad32645a9.png)

In general,

$$
X_i = \{ i \} \times [0, i^2] = \big\{ (i,k) \: : \: k \in [0, i^2] \big\}
$$

is the vertical line segment from the point $(i,0)$ to the point $(i, i^2).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040430/assets/60c98be5d97748e9285bb5e9c30bba9781a5ef99245789718a7828b18a6df8fb.png)

 

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following figure that represents the union $\displaystyle \bigcup_{i \in I} X_i{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040430/assets/b3a61d686c78c76a4f461c1c771437d31030339b634661da8b8dc4f492db55eb.png)

e-13321.knowledge_point: Visualizing Intersections of Uncountable Families of Indexed Sets
e-13321.problem: Let $I = [0,1] \subset \mathbb{R}$ and $X_i = [-i, 0] \times [-1,1].$ Sketch a representation of $\displaystyle \bigcap_{i \in I} X_i$ in the Cartesian plane.
e-13321.worked_solution:
Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
\bigcap_{i \in I} A_i = \big\{ x \: : \: x \in A_k \:\:\textrm{for all}\:\: k \in I \big\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
X_{0.5} = [-0.5,0] \times [-1, 1] = \big\{ (a,b) \: : \: a \in [-0.5, 0], b \in [-1, 1] \big\}.
$$

This represents a rectangle whose vertices are at $(-0.5, -1),$ $(-0.5, 1),$ $(0, 1),$ and $(0, -1)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040430/assets/8ad650cb3f2fa4da920a442e8cc1b24af5027595cba4e43138eff2126cf4c102.png)

In general,

$$
X_i = [-i, 0] \times [-1,1] = \big\{ (a,b) \: : \: a \in [-i, 0], b \in [-1, 1] \big\}
$$

is the rectangle whose vertices are at $(-i,-1),$ $(-i,1),$ $(0, 1),$ and $(0, -1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040430/assets/a37cfa508cf3a60536084fbc1e57c5aeac3414904d2ad72ef1deda85dc4eddd8.png)

 

The intersection of all these rectangles is the line segment $\{0\}\times [-1,1]{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040430/assets/5e9a611629f4370c57e77a057439c759670afa17c14c4b2339e1d471f616ea72.png)

The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B={(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B}
$$

In this case, the set

$$
S=R\times [-1,1]
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1].$

$$
S={(x,y)\,:\,x\in R,\,y\in [-1,1]}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{0}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $0$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1].$

$$
{S}_{0}={(0,y)\,:\,y\in [-1,1]}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{0}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040430/assets/588f2574b1aaf0e96895816ca34bd9c6900a9b13342f44bd4104ad2bf4270bf5.png)

Now, consider a general ${S}_{i}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals some $i\in R$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1].$

$$
{S}_{i}={(i,y)\,:\,y\in [-1,1]}
$$

For each $i\in R,$ ${S}_{i}$ is a vertical line segment from the point $(i,-1)$ to the point $(i,1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040430/assets/8458978c2766d899b03149de53739650932875d6463c25dd3bbde99bc6a71ea7.png)

Our Cartesian product $S$ is the union of these subsets over $R:$

$$
S={⋃}_{i\in R}{S}_{i}.
$$

As $i$ runs over $R,$ these line segments sweep the following bar that represents the union ${⋃}_{i\in R}{S}_{i}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040430/assets/6fc81e487503ce86d3bf5366e57db087484e8bd1e8bafd52738c65e8e173c387.png)

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for at least one}\,\,k\in I}
$$

$$
{X}_{0.5}={0.5}\times [0,0.125]={(0.5,k)\,:\,k\in [0,0.125]}.
$$

$$
{X}_{i}={i}\times [0,{i}^{3}]={(i,k)\,:\,k\in [0,{i}^{3}]}

is the vertical line segment from the point $(i,0)$ to the point $(i,{i}^{3}).$
